body:
Six top-2 teams have already fallen, fueling comparisons to 2007 and raising questions about whether parity is reshaping college football
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:59 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The 2007 college football season is the gold standard for chaotic years in the sport, as a top-2 ranking in the AP poll became a curse rather than a reward. A top-2-ranked team in the AP poll lost in five consecutive weeks to end the 2007 season, which remains the all-time record, and, overall, either No. 1 or No. 2 in the country lost an astounding 11 times over the course of the season. The period of relative stability at the top of the college football world that followed that legendary 2007 campaign made many wonder if we'd ever see anything like it again. Well, 19 years later, we have our hands on another season where the only certainty seems to be chaos at the top. October 2026 will go down as a historic one. The five losses by AP top-2 teams are tied for the most in a single month since November 2007 -- October 2007 also saw four such losses -- and it's also the first time since November 2007 that the No. 1 and No. 2 teams in the AP poll finished the month with a losing record (4-5). 
2007 vs. 202620072026Week 6: Stanford 24, No. 2 USC 23 Week 3: No. 4 Texas 24, No. 1 Ohio State 23Week 7: No. 17 Kentucky 43, No. 1 LSU 37Week 7: Oklahoma 27, No. 1 Texas 24Week 7: Oregon State 31, No. 2 Cal 28Week 8: Auburn 27, No. 1 Georgia 24Week 8: Rutgers 30, No. 2 South Florida 27Week 8: No. 8 BYU 28, No. 2 Notre Dame 24Week 10: Florida State 27, No. 2 Boston College 17Week 9: UCF 39, No. 2 BYU 31Week 11: Illinois 28, No. 1 Ohio State 21Week 10: USC 30, No. 2 Ohio State 18Week 12: Arizona 34, No. 2 Oregon 24???Week 13: Arkansas 50, No. 1 LSU 48???Week 13: No. 3 Missouri 36, No. 2 Kansas 28???Week 14: No. 9 Oklahoma 38, No. 1 Missouri 17???Week 14: Pittsburgh 13, No. 2 West Virginia 9???As the calendar turns to November, six different teams ranked No. 1 or No. 2 have lost, marking the most top-2 losses before November since 1984 -- 1981 is the only season with more top-2 losses before November (7). Five of those losses have come in the last four weeks, which means with another loss on Saturday, 2007 will suddenly have company for the most consecutive weeks with a top-2 team losing. That possibility is not at all far-fetched considering what the schedule provides in Week 10. No. 1 Miami and No. 2 Georgia each go on the road to face a top-12 ranked opponent (No. 4 Notre Dame and No. 12 Ole Miss, respectively), meaning there is a very real chance the top of the polls get shaken up again going into Week 11.The Hurricanes have already had to pull off late escapes against a pair of unranked opponents in recent weeks, while the Bulldogs showed their vulnerability in a stunning loss to Auburn after grabbing the No. 1 ranking. The lack of a clearly dominant top tier in the sport has created a void that no one can seemingly fill for very long at the top of the rankings. 
        
            
                CBS Sports 138: Utah surges, joins Miami and Georgia in top three of college football rankings
                
                    Chip Patterson                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The anatomy of a chaos seasonWhat makes the 2007 season stand out isn't just how many top-ranked teams lost, but some of the programs that put on their wings of wax and flew a bit too close to the sun. There were certainly blue-bloods and traditional powers like LSU, Ohio State and USC (and an early version of Oregon), but seeing Missouri, Kansas, South Florida, Boston College and West Virginia all grab a brief hold of a top-2 ranking made the season that much more fun. The 2026 season hasn't quite reached that level yet, with Ohio State, Georgia, Notre Dame and Texas accounting for five of the losses, but we aren't that many steps away from getting there. Utah and UCLA are undefeated top-5 teams currently and could be in line to jump in if Miami or Georgia falls this weekend. Kentucky and Wake Forest are ranked No. 8 and No. 14 respectively, and if things get weird enough, perhaps a one-loss version of the Wildcats or Demon Deacons could sniff the top-2 -- not to mention we're all still getting used to "college football powerhouse Indiana" being part of this current reality. There's also the importance of who is beating the top teams in fostering that sense of chaos. In 2007, eight of the 11 losses by top-2 teams came against unranked opponents. It wasn't a matter of the schedule presenting tons of ranked-on-ranked battles with the same teams cannibalizing each other. Instead, there was the feeling that every week something unexpected wasn't just possible but would happen. The 2026 season has had a similar vibe, even with talent consolidating into the power conferences. The SEC and Big Ten make up most of the top 25, but this year has still seen four of the six top-2 losses come against unranked opponents. While Week 10 will present a pair of top-12 matchups for No. 1 and No. 2, there is a sense that the talent gap between the very top and the middle tier of college football is smaller than it's been in quite some time. The era after 2007, dominated by Nick Saban at Alabama, saw the top teams consolidate talent on a few rosters. Now, while talent still finds its way to the top conferences, it's much harder to go two- or three-deep across the depth chart with elite players because it's easier than ever for players to find someone who will play them (and pay them) immediately. Perhaps the best example of that is the backup-quarterback crisis across the sport, where teams rarely have a steady backup ready to go because a quality backup at an elite program typically lands a starting job somewhere in college football's middle class. Whether the parity of this season is a trend to watch in college football going forward or just a wild outlier remains to be seen, but if nothing else, it has produced the most exciting and unpredictable season in nearly two decades. With a full month of football left to be played, there's still plenty of time for chaos to reign, and as the College Football Playoff committee gets set to begin its weekly rankings, nothing feels like a certainty.

title: MLB proposes delaying salary cap in new negotiations as Dec. 1 CBA expiration inches nearer - CBS Sports
description: In the league's new proposal, the salary cap would not be instituted until the 2028 season to give teams time to
body:
In the league's new proposal, the salary cap would not be instituted until the 2028 season to give teams time to prepare
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:59 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the implementation of a salary cap/floor system until 2028 as part of its latest collective bargaining agreement proposal, the league announced Tuesday. MLB says the delay is intended to provide a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system and give teams more time to prepare and get their payrolls in order."We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool, and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."The league also newly proposed a $180.2 million salary floor and a $258.2 million salary cap. Those numbers are up from $171.2 million and $245.3 million, respectively, in the league's previous proposal in June. The $1 million minimum salary would only apply to players with at least two years of service time. The minimum salary would be $900,000 for all other players.Four teams currently have more than $258.2 million on the books for 2027 (including arbitration projections) and 20 teams have less than $180.2 million on the books, according to FanGraphs' calculations. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027 before the transition to a salary cap/floor system in 2028.
The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time. The previous lockout ended on March 10, then there was a three-week spring training leading up to Opening Day. If there is a similarly lengthy lockout, it would be impossible for clubs to become salary cap-compliant in such a short period of time.The MLB Players Association has repeatedly insisted it will not accept a salary cap/floor system, and has instead proposed a revised revenue sharing system that would funnel more money from big-market teams to small-market teams. In a statement following the league's proposal on Tuesday, the MLBPA accused owners of continuing to "propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The union also said that even with a delayed implementation, the league's proposal of a salary cap maintains the same "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights, including guaranteed contracts."
MLB says its push for a salary cap/floor system is intended to improve competitive balance. The small-market Milwaukee Brewers defeated the small-market Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series last week and swept big-market teams (Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees) en route to the Fall Classic.

title: MLB rumors: How Yankees could make a Tarik Skubal deal work, plus Mets' priority and a Rangers pivot - CBS Sports
description: With free agency officially underway, here's the latest from the offseason hot stove
body:
With free agency officially underway, here's the latest from the offseason hot stove
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:34 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The 2026-27 MLB offseason is less than one week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Tuesday's hot stove happenings.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
      Yankees could pursue Skubal, trade a starter  
The Yankees are at least considering a run at Tarik Skubal, by far the best available free agent, and then trading another starting pitcher to address needs elsewhere on the roster, reports ESPN. New York is one of the few teams in baseball that legitimately does not need to add to its rotation this offseason, though there is no such thing as too much pitching.  This is the club's rotation depth chart at the moment:  RHP Cam SchlittlerLHP Max FriedRHP Gerrit ColeLHP Carlos RodónLHP Ryan WeathersRHP Will WarrenRHP Clarke Schmidt (missed most of 2026 following UCL surgery)RHP Elmer RodríguezSchlittler and the well-paid veterans aren't going anywhere. Warren is the most sensible trade chip. He threw 156 innings with a 3.92 ERA and solid under-the-hood indicators this past season and has four years of team control remaining. Cheap, controllable pitching is the game's greatest currency. It's always in demand and it can get you anything you need in a trade.  The Yankees need help at second and third base this offseason, possibly in center field and at catcher as well. Signing Skubal (or a different veteran) and trading Warren for help on the position player side is a sensible strategy for New York.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
     Mets focused on rotation upgrades The Mets are focused on adding to their rotation and are "active everywhere," according to The Athletic. They're looking at the top of the market (i.e. Tarik Skubal) as well as at the small army of solid veterans who occupy the middle tier of the free agent class. The Mets could also explore the trade market, though the team is said to not be keen on dealing prospects this offseason. At the moment, Nolan McLean and Christian Scott are the only locks for New York's 2027 rotation. Here is the team's starting pitching depth chart: RHP Nolan McLeanRHP Christian ScottLHP Zac ThorntonRHP Kodai SengaLHP Sean ManaeaRHP Tylor Megill (missed 2026 following UCL surgery)RHP Jonah TongRHP Tobias MyersRHP Justin HagenmanSenga could return to the bullpen after pitching admirably in the closer's role late this year. Clearly, the Mets need at least one starter this offseason and could really use more than one, just to lessen the reliance on young pitchers like Thornton and Tong. President of baseball operations David Stearns is disinclined to give pitchers long-term deals, which could put the Mets at a disadvantage for Skubal. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
      Rangers prioritizing center field  
Gold Glove finalist Evan Carter underwent right hip surgery last week and will miss the start of the 2027 season, Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young announced Monday. As a result, Texas will prioritize center field help this offseason. If needed, the Rangers can put left fielder Wyatt Langford (also a Gold Glove finalist) in center, but Langford is best in left.  "There's no doubt that we have to be cognizant that Evan's coming off a major surgery, and that we're going to have to find potential backfills if he is not ready to start the season, or if there are any setbacks," Young said, via MLB.com. "It doesn't change our belief in Evan long term, but it does change our short-term plans that we need to have a backfill and somebody who can certainly fill in or play a very solid center field and hopefully contribute offensively." The free agent class does not offer much in center field unless you're willing to take on injury or age-related decline risk. Here are the top available free agent center fielders according to FanGraphs projected 2027 WAR:  
Trent Grisham: 2.1 WARLuis Robert Jr.: 1.6 WARDaulton Varsho: 1.3 WARCedric Mullins: 1.2 WARTyrone Taylor: 0.8 WARJarren Duran (Red Sox) and Steven Kwan (Guardians) stand out as center field trade candidates, though Kwan in particular will come at a high price. A cheaper, defense-first stopgap like, say, Denzel Clarke (Athletics) or Blake Perkins (Guardians) may be the best short-term option while Carter is on the mend.

title: Jerry Jones' coaching philosophy explains why Cowboys can't end playoff drought - CBS Sports
description: The Cowboys owner insists coaching investment has no correlation with winning
body:
The Cowboys owner insists coaching investment has no correlation with winning
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:52 am ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Dallas Cowboys are the NFL's highest-profile team. They are "America's Team." They are the most valuable franchise in the league, according to the various outlets that determine franchise valuations. They get the highest ratings on TV. They anchor the most segments on sports talk shows, and they generate more online discourse than anyone.And yet, they are not the most successful franchise in the league, or even close to it. They infamously have not even been to the NFC title game since the 1995 season, after which they won their third Super Bowl in four years. They have the 11th-best regular-season record during that time, but the fourth-worst postseason record. The last 30-plus years have shown that the Cowboys do not know how to win when the stakes are highest. And yet, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones refuses to change how he does business. He is the "general manager" of the team, and that will not change. He runs the team his way, and that will not change. He gives interviews to the local media following the game, even before the head coach or players speak to the press, and that will not change. He goes on the radio multiple times per week, and that will not change.
And he doesn't even attempt to hire the best coaches for his team, because he doesn't think that doing so it worth it from a financial perspective, and that will not change. Just ask Jones himself, who attempted to justify that stance during a radio interview on Tuesday."There is zero correlation (in the NFL) between how much you pay a coach or how many coaches you have as to winning," Jones said on 105.3 The Fan, via The Athletic. "There is no correlation. And that's a random sample of years and all 32 teams involved. So put that in your hopper and smoke it."Coaching salaries, for the most part, aren't made public, so we can't actually find out whether there is a correlation between coaching salaries and winning. What we do know is that good coaches tend to win more games than bad ones, all else equal, and that good coaches generally cost more to hire than bad ones. 
And now we know what we have long suspected: Jones simply isn't willing to pay for the best candidates. It's no wonder the Cowboys haven't done much winning since Jerry unceremoniously parted ways with the best coach he ever hired, Jimmy Johnson. Jones famously fumed that Johnson got more credit for the Cowboys' success during their early-1990s heyday than did Jones himself, and drove Johnson away from the franchise amid their feud. Jones quipped at the time that "any of 500 coaches could have won a Super Bowl" with the roster the Cowboys had, and he has been trying to prove it ever since.Jones has barely pretended to run coaching searches the last few times the Cowboys have had a coach opening, stacking the deck for candidates like Jason Garrett, Mike McCarthy and Brian Schottenheimer — go-along-to-get-along types who would let Jerry by Jerry and not rock the boat too much.
The Cowboys had an opening two years ago, when Ben Johnson — who was considered arguably the best coaching candidate in years and who has since revitalized the Chicago Bears — was available, and they did not even request an interview with him. At the same time, Mike Vrabel — a renowned culture-setter, despite this past offseason's indiscretions — was available, and they did not even request an interview with him. At the same time, Liam Coen — an offensive innovator who has taken the Jacksonville Jaguars to new heights — was available, and they did not even request an interview with him. At the same time, Brian Flores — arguably the best defensive coach in the league — was available, and they did not even request an interview with him. The list goes on and on, and the Cowboys interviewed candidates that, for the most part, nobody else in the league was interested in at the time. (Only two of the six publicly-revealed candidates were interviewed by other teams that offseason.)Jones does not care to hire the best coach available because he does not want to pay what it takes to hire the best coach and he does not want to share credit with the coach if the Cowboys ever manage to win anything substantial. And it's a big part of the reason why they won't.

title: Why Bears' Caleb Williams gave up his fight against the NFL over his unapproved cleats - CBS Sports
description: For the first time this season, Caleb Williams actually followed the NFL's uniform policy
body:
For the first time this season, Caleb Williams actually followed the NFL's uniform policy
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:02 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        After taking on the NFL over the past two weeks and getting hit with more than $35,000 in fines, Caleb Williams has finally given up the fight over his cleats. During Chicago's 34-17 win over the Seahawks on Monday, Williams covered up the logo on his Caddix cleats for the first time this season. Following the game, the Bears quarterback said he gave in because he didn't want it to be a distraction anymore. "Just to calm things down," Williams said after the game. "It was a big week and not here to create any B.S. towards the team. I want to keep that to a minimum from my side. Obviously I get a lot of media and so just trying to minimize that as much as possible."All eyes were on Williams going into Monday's game because he was heading into uncharted territory. Under NFL rules, there are only three companies that currently have a partnership with the NFL — Nike, Adidas and Under Armour — and the logos from those three companies are the only ones that are allowed to be on the field during a game. 
Players are allowed to wear a pair of cleats from a different company, but if they go that route, they have to cover up the logo. Williams has been wearing his Caddix cleats all season and the NFL finally hit him with a $11,941 fine in Week 6. In Week 7, not only did Williams wear the cleats again, but once again, he knowingly violated NFL protocols by not covering up the logo. The league responded by hitting him with a $23,882 fine. After being fined $35,823 over two weeks, Williams still wasn't ready to back down. In the lead-up to Monday's game against the Seahawks, he actually told ESPN that he would not be covering the logo on his cleats. The problem with that plan is that the NFL is actually allowed to keep a player from participating in a game if the player keeps violating the league's uniform policy, so there was a chance that Williams wouldn't be allowed to play if he didn't cover up his cleats for Monday's game. Williams clearly got the message, because when he came out for warmups, the Caddix logo was covered up. 
Bears coach Ben Johnson was asked about the cleat controversy over the weekend and he seemed pretty confident that his star QB was going to make the right decision. "He's all about the team and I know he's not going to hurt the team," Johnson said last Saturday.Williams wears the Caddix cleats because he thinks they're safer than other brands. 
"As we've known for the past couple of years now, I'm huge into my body, I'm huge into trying to stay on the field, I'm huge into trying to be healthy," Williams said last week. "It's a rough game and things like that. The cleats, they've been great, they've been super comfy and they've worked. They are a science type of cleat."The Caddix cleats, which are known for their patented "SmartStuds" technology, are now worn by dozens of NFL players. Joe Flacco was the first NFL player to wear them back in 2024, and he liked them so much that he's now an investor in the company. He actually offered to pay any fines that Williams might incur for getting them. Caddix also offered to pay the QB's fines, according to ESPN, so there's a good chance that the Bears QB won't end up losing out any money despite getting fined more than $35,000.

title: Cowboys' Jerry Jones has blunt response on George Pickens' useage: 'He needs the ball coming his way more' - CBS Sports
description: Pickens is coming off his lowest snap count since being traded to Dallas
body:
Pickens is coming off his lowest snap count since being traded to Dallas
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:24 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        It's a good thing Jerry Jones likes talking, because there are plenty of questions to answer in Dallas given the Cowboys' 3-5 start. One of the biggest questions in Dallas has been George Pickens' lack of involvement in the Cowboys' offense over the past two weeks. Pickens caught just two passes and was on the field for only 57% of Dallas' offensive snaps during Sunday's overtime loss to the Cardinals. Conversely, fellow wideout Ryan Flournoy played in 68% of the team's offensive snaps. Jones, the Cowboys' owner, president and general manager, was asked point-blank on 105.3 The Fan about Pickens' disappearing act on Sunday. Jones attributed Pickens' lack of involvement to the team's offensive plan. "He needs the ball coming his way more, and there's your good case," Jones said. "You say what can you do differently than we did out there the other day? We get the ball in that direction more, and we press that. We had a really firm game plan to come out there and run that ball. 
"We ran the ball, I think, 39 times, and we just didn't get it done. And the Arizona line is to be commended. They did not have that reputation to be able to have the kind of game that they had against us. So that's one of the frustrating things about that game."Dallas did run the ball 39 times but for just 93 yards. When Dak Prescott did drop back to pass, the majority of his targets went to CeeDee Lamb, who was targeted 11 times. Pickens was targeted just four times. Flournoy received more snaps than Pickens on Sunday because he is a more willing blocker in the running game. Pickens' talent -- especially as a pass-catcher -- is undeniable, but his effort on plays that don't involve him continues to be an issue. 
Pickens' lack of a complete game is currently costing him snaps in Dallas. It may also cost him a long-term contract with the Cowboys, who could decide to trade him ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline if Dallas loses Sunday's game to the Indianapolis Colts, who are also in the middle of a tumultuous season.

Sunday's injury took place during the first half when Love was tackled by multiple Cowboys defenders.

With Love out, the Cardinals will lean more on Tyler Allgeier, who leads Arizona with 323 yards on the ground. Formerly Bijan Robinson's backup in Atlanta, Allgeier amassed 191 total yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's win over Dallas.

title: 2026 midseason rookie grades: Ranking the early hits, misses and biggest surprises - CBS Sports
description: Eight weeks into the NFL season, we're starting to get some answers about the 2026 first-round rookie class. Some players look exactly l
body:
Eight weeks into the NFL season, we're starting to get some answers about the 2026 first-round rookie class. Some players look exactly like we thought they would when they came out of college. Others have been pleasant surprises. And then there are those still struggling with some of the same issues that showed up on their college tape.We evaluated these rookies after four weeks on the With the First Pick podcast – it was our most popular episode this fall – and Arvell Reese and Sonny Styles were among the early standouts. David Bailey was still finding his footing, Rueben Bain Jr. was battling injuries, and Dillon Thieneman looked like one of the league's most promising young safeties.
A month later, some of those evaluations look a little (and, in some cases, a lot) different.These are our first-half grades for all 32 first-round picks from the 2026 class, based on everything we've seen through eight weeks. Production matters, but so do injuries, expectations and what the tape reveals. We're also revisiting our original scouting reports from the 2026 draft cycle to see which traits have translated, which concerns have followed these players to the NFL, and where we might have missed something. And because good players aren't limited to the first round, we've also graded 10 rookies drafted on Days 2 and 3 who have already made their mark.
1. Fernando Mendoza, QB, Raiders: INCOMPLETEMendoza finally got on the field in Week 5 mop-up duty vs. the Patriots. He was a tidy 6 of 8 for 48 yards. For now, veteran Kirk Cousins remains the starter, but as the losses pile up, Mendoza will likely get his chance to be QB1.2. David Bailey, EDGE, Jets: BBailey has taken a noticeable step forward after an uneven start, highlighted by a three-sack performance against Cleveland. I loved his explosive first step, speed-to-power, inside spin and relentless motor at Texas Tech, and we're seeing all of it in the NFL. What's been particularly encouraging is his development against the run, where Jets coaches have praised his discipline and ability to handle responsibilities beyond rushing the passer. He's becoming the complete defender New York envisioned when it drafted him second overall.3. Jeremiyah Love, RB, Cardinals: C+Love hasn't looked like the explosive, home-run threat we watched at Notre Dame, but there's a very simple reason: He's been battling an ankle injury since the preseason, and it cost him two games. At Notre Dame, I loved his ability to accelerate through the smallest crease and turn ordinary runs into big plays, but Love has acknowledged that he hasn't been able to cut or explode the way he did in college (not yet, anyway). This grade really doesn't mean much until we see what a healthy version of Love looks like. And that won't be for at least another month with today's trip to the IR.
4. Carnell Tate, WR, Titans: BTate is becoming a dependable target for Cam Ward despite Tennessee's offensive struggles, and that's hardly surprising given how polished he looked at Ohio State. His ability to manipulate DBs, separate at the top of routes and make difficult catches look easy gave him a chance to contribute immediately. Tate continues to get more comfortable in Tennessee's offense, and he's showing the makings of a No. 1 receiver.5. Arvell Reese, LB, Giants: A+Remember all those concerns about Reese's pro day workout? Seven months later and he's one of the easiest evaluations in the class because he's doing exactly what made him such an exciting prospect at Ohio State. Instincts, range, and insane athleticism, while learning on the job, have all made him an immediate difference-maker, and Giants coaches have praised how quickly he's hit the ground running.6. Mansoor Delane, CB, Chiefs: A-Delane looked like a grizzled All-Pro from the moment he stepped on the field. The only issue has been staying healthy. He was one of the most technically sound CBs in the draft and that has immediately translated – even when he's "allowed" receptions while in coverage (show me the human who is stopping JSN – also, look at Delane's coverage!). The Chiefs traded up for Delane and so far, it appears that they nailed this pick.
7. Sonny Styles, LB, Commanders: A+Washington already trusts Styles to relay defensive calls and make adjustments before the snap, impressive responsibilities for a rookie still relatively new to playing off-ball LB. His instincts and athleticism stood out at Ohio State, and he's carried those strengths into the NFL. He's been particularly effective in coverage vs. TEs and RBs, and he's shown consistent improvement against the run. There have been occasional missed tackles, but through eight weeks, he's been one of the best players in this rookie class.8. Jordyn Tyson, WR, Saints: INCOMPLETEThe issue with Tyson in college was staying healthy. Those issues remain.9. Spencer Fano, OT, Browns: A-Cleveland appears to have found its long-term answer at left tackle. Fano's footwork, balance and ability to recover against high-end edge rushers were some of the reasons I liked him so much coming out of Utah. And even though he's moved from right to left tackle for the Browns, he's doing a lot of the same things really well. 10. Francis Mauigoa, OG, Giants: C+The move from college tackle to NFL guard hasn't been seamless, but Mauigoa has steadily gotten better. His athleticism and ability to move defenders in the running game stood out at Miami, although he occasionally struggled with balance and hand placement. Those issues have followed him inside, but his improved pass protection, especially vs. Houston in Week 7, was encouraging.
11. Caleb Downs, S, Cowboys: C+Few prospects were easier to trust coming out of college than Downs, whose instincts, anticipation and IQ made him special at Ohio State. This is what makes his recent NFL struggles so surprising (I gave him a B+ through the first month of the season). Opponents have completed 20 of 24 passes against him for 230 yards and three touchdowns, and poor pursuit angles have contributed to explosive runs. Dallas expected a defensive centerpiece, not a liability in coverage, as CBS Sports' Garrett Podell detailed.12. Kadyn Proctor, OG, Dolphins: C+Proctor has been candid about his struggles moving inside, acknowledging that speed of the game in confined spaces -- something he didn't have to deal with at Alabama -- creates bigger problems at guard. His rare athleticism remains obvious, but the balance and hand-placement concerns from his college tape haven't disappeared. A Week 7 concussion hasn't helped, keeping him sidelined for Week 8's loss to the Patriots.13. Ty Simpson, QB, Rams: INCOMPLETERemember when we all gawked and pointed at the Rams' arrogance for taking Simpson when there were bigger, more immediate needs? I suppose that case can still be made … but it also doesn't look like Matthew Stafford has another year or two left in him. 
14. Olaivavega Ioane, OG, Ravens: B+Baltimore has already needed Ioane to play center because of injuries, and he's handled the transition well. His powerful hands, leverage and ability to anchor made him one of my favorite interior linemen at Penn State. He's brought that same reliability to Baltimore, although an MCL injury has interrupted an otherwise encouraging start. And while our old buddy Rick Spielman wasn't a fan of plus/minus when grading players, I'm giving Ioane an extra plus for his versatility. 15. Rueben Bain Jr., EDGE, Buccaneers: CIt's taken a bit, but we're finally seeing the player who was a game wrecker at Miami. Shoulder and groin injuries derailed Bain's first month, but his explosive first step, violent hands and ability to generate power are showing up more consistently as he gets healthy. The production hasn't matched expectations yet, although he's trending in the right direction.16. Kenyon Sadiq, TE, Jets: B-Remember Sadiq's seven-catch, 105-yard performance against Detroit? That's the explosive mismatch weapon we saw at Oregon. But his opportunities have diminished with Mason Taylor back in the lineup, and a Week 5 concussion only complicated matters. The encouraging part? His blocking has been better than expected, even if the receiving production hasn't followed.
17. Blake Miller, OT, Lions: BMiller's pass protection has been one of the more encouraging developments among all rookie offensive linemen. His balance, lateral agility and ability to redirect stood out at Clemson, and he's handled NFL edge rushers surprisingly well over the first two months. The running game is another story; he hasn't been nearly as good play in and play out.18. Caleb Banks, DT, Vikings: INCOMPLETEMinnesota knew Banks was a developmental prospect, but he's played just 25% of the defensive snaps and hasn't made much of an impact. When healthy, his twitch, lateral quickness and ability to penetrate made him a lot of fun to watch at Florida. The problem? Once blockers get their hands on him, particularly on double teams, he struggles to disengage. Those concerns haven't disappeared, and his limited playing time suggests the Vikings aren't ready to trust him with a bigger role. I'm giving Banks an incomplete here, in part because we knew this would be a process, in part because Dallas Turner needed a couple of years in Brian Flores' system before figuring it out.19. Monroe Freeling, OT, Panthers: C-Freeling deserves credit for responding well when Carolina needed him earlier than expected, and at a position (RT) he didn't play in college. A knee injury hasn't helped his development,  and right now, he's more of a developmental prospect than a reliable starter.
20. Makai Lemon, WR, Eagles: B-After a quiet September that left a lot of folks wondering if Sean Mannion knew Lemon was on the roster, the USC standout is finally starting to look like the first-round talent we saw last fall for the Trojans. His toughness, reliable hands and ability to create after the catch have become more evident as his role expands. There have been some drops, but he's one of the few bright spots in an otherwise forgettable season in Philly.21. Max Iheanachor, OT, Steelers: B-Iheanachor hasn't avoided rookie mistakes, but what's encouraging is how he's responded to them. His quick feet, power and lateral movement skills were obvious at Arizona State, even if he was incredibly raw. He's still raw, but he's shown an ability to quickly make adjustments instead of repeating the same mistakes.22. Akheem Mesidor, EDGE, Chargers: BDespite all that's gone wrong with the Chargers, Mesidor has been one of the bright spots, and his coaches have explained why: he's stopped overthinking and started trusting his instincts. The heavy hands, leverage, versatility and non-stop motor that made him a first-rounder out of Miami are showing up more consistently. He's playing faster, even if the production doesn't always reflect it.
23. Malachi Lawrence, EDGE, Cowboys: C-Lawrence's first NFL sack offered a glimpse of the explosiveness that made him stand out at UCF. His first-step quickness and power were impressive in college, but limited bend meant he'd need to develop better counters and hand usage. That's all still a work in progress, and the reality is that Dallas hasn't gotten consistent production from him. In his defense, they've gotten consistent production from exactly no one on this defense.24. KC Concepcion, WR, Browns: B+Concepcion has been better than advertised and the advertisements were pretty good coming out of Texas A&M. His suddenness and precise route running have immediately translated. Browns coaches have also praised his preparation and ability to learn multiple receiver positions, giving Cleveland more ways to get him involved. GM Andrew Berry has quietly crushed another draft class.25. Dillon Thieneman, S, Bears: B-A month ago, Thieneman looked like one of the pleasant surprises of Round 1 (I gave him a B+ at the quarter pole). His instincts, range and willingness to attack downhill were everything we saw at Oregon. But the concerns about flipping his hips and tracking receivers downfield have resurfaced, and now opponents are increasingly testing him vertically. His second month hasn't been nearly as impressive as his first, but there's still a ton to be excited about.
26. Keylan Rutledge, OG, Texans: C-Houston drafted Rutledge to add some much-needed nastiness up front, but his pass protection has been a problem. To be fair, the Texans have asked him to learn all three interior o-line positions after playing almost exclusively right guard at Georgia Tech. Still, poor balance, hand placement and recognition have made him vulnerable, and the physical tools remain more impressive than the results. Overall, I'm going to grade him on a curve because he's been asked to do a lot in a short span.27. Chris Johnson, CB, Dolphins: C+Johnson is becoming more dependable as Miami moves him between outside corner and the slot. His competitiveness, recovery speed and ability to stay in phase on shorter routes were strengths at San Diego State, and we're seeing that now show up on Sundays. Bottom line: He's made real progress since September, when I gave him a C.28. Caleb Lomu, OT, Patriots: INCOMPLETELomu has played only about 160 snaps -- far fewer than most of the first-round rookie offensive linemen -- but he's made the most of his opportunities. He was impressive against the Jets in Week 6. Filling in for an injured Morgan Moses, he played 60 snaps at right tackle, allowed zero pressures and held his own against David Bailey. His quick feet and balance were strengths at Utah, and they're serving him well as he adjusts to the NFL. I gave him an incomplete here but if pressed, I'd give him a B-.29. Peter Woods, DT, Chiefs: C+Woods was one of the most physically gifted defenders in this class, which makes his uneven start a little frustrating. His explosiveness, leverage and ability to disrupt running plays have translated from Clemson, but he hasn't been nearly as effective rushing the passer. He still struggles with double teams, and his inability to consistently win one-on-one as a pass rusher remains a concern.30. Omar Cooper Jr., WR, Jets: A-Two consecutive 100-yard games after returning from injured reserve? That'll work. Cooper's toughness, contested-catch ability and knack for making difficult receptions look routine were how he made his name at Indiana. He's already developing chemistry with Geno Smith, and while it's a small sample, there's a lot to like.31. Keldric Faulk, EDGE, Titans: D+Faulk's length and power made him an appealing first-round prospect at Auburn, but he hasn't consistently turned those tools into on-field production. An early sack against the Giants offered a glimpse of his potential. Since then, he's struggled when OTs have neutralized his initial pass-rush move. He'll need to diversify his pass-rush arsenal, something that showed up on tape in college but was less of an issue because he was routinely the freakiest athlete on the field. 32. Jadarian Price, RB, Seahawks: INCOMPLETEPrice's chest injury has left us with little to evaluate. He got off to a promising start in Week 1, rushing for 52 yards on 10 carries, but played just two more games before landing on injured reserve. He also lost fumbles in both of those appearances. The talent we saw at Notre Dame is still there, but we've barely seen it in Seattle.Of course, the first round isn't the only place teams find impact players. Here are some Day 2 names who have stood out through the first half of their rookie seasons -- and in some cases, are already outperforming players drafted well ahead of them.Beyond the first round: Ten more rookies already making a markDenzel Boston, WR, Browns (Round 2): B+Boston has given Cleveland a legitimate downfield threat, with 409 receiving yards and three touchdowns through eight games. His size, body control and ability to win contested catches have translated from Washington, although defenses have done a better job limiting his explosive plays recently.Jacob Rodriguez, LB, Dolphins (Round 2): A-Rodriguez has wasted little time becoming an important part of Miami's defense, relying on the instincts, play recognition and tackling ability that made him so productive at Texas Tech. He may not have elite athletic traits, but he consistently finds the football and has been one of the more impressive second-round rookies.Gabe Jacas, EDGE, Patriots (Round 2): A-Jacas has been a problem for opposing offensive tackles, generating 21 pressures through his first seven games. His power, bend and ability to diagnose plays have stood out on film, and he's already producing like a player who should have been drafted higher.Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, S, Browns (Round 2): B+McNeil-Warren has earned an expanding role in Cleveland's secondary, where his length, physicality, closing speed and versatility have helped the Browns disguise coverages. The instincts and willingness to attack downhill that stood out at Toledo are serving him well, and he's developing into a valuable piece of the defense.Germie Bernard, WR, Steelers (Round 2): B+Bernard has taken advantage of Pittsburgh's injuries at receiver, becoming an increasingly reliable target for Aaron Rodgers. His route awareness, toughness, blocking and ability to line up in multiple spots have translated from Alabama, while his preparation and willingness to learn have earned praise from the coaching staff.And then there are the Day 3 picks, where finding immediate contributors becomes a little more difficult -- and sometimes the evaluations look a lot different with the benefit of hindsight. For these five rookies, I've included my original pre-draft grade, final big board ranking and what I liked about them coming out of college, if only to see what I got right, what I missed and whether these teams saw something I didn't.Gracen Halton, DT, 49ers (Round 4): A-My pre-draft grade: 3rd–4th round | Final big board rank: No. 98Why I liked him: An explosive, one-gap penetrator with surprising power, active hands and a relentless motor who could disrupt plays before offensive linemen established their blocks.Halton has been one of the biggest Day 3 steals, making an immediate impact on San Francisco's defensive line with 15 tackles, two sacks and a forced fumble through six games. His first-step quickness, ability to disengage from blockers and relentless motor have all helped him become an integral part of the rotation.Keionte Scott, DB, Buccaneers (Round 4): A-My pre-draft grade: 3rd round | Final big board rank: No. 84Why I liked him: A physical, aggressive slot defender who could cover, blitz off the edge and blow up running plays near the line of scrimmage.Scott might be the best example of a Day 3 rookie playing well beyond his draft position (though he slipped on draft day because of off-field concerns). He's already established himself as Tampa Bay's starting nickel, where his physicality, quick trigger and versatility have made him a valuable part of Todd Bowles' defense. Bowles has praised his toughness and tackling.Dani Dennis-Sutton, EDGE, Packers (Round 4): B+My pre-draft grade: 4th round | Final big board rank: No. 122Why I liked him: A powerful, high-motor edge defender with heavy hands, a strong lower half and the ability to set the edge against the run.Dennis-Sutton has given Green Bay valuable pass-rush production, generating 15 pressures through seven weeks and earning more playing time as a result. His power, heavy hands and ability to hold up against the run were obvious at Penn State, but he's also shown more as a pass rusher than I expected.Jaden Dugger, LB, 49ers (Round 5): B+My pre-draft grade: 7th–UDFA | Final big board rank: No. 300Why I liked him: A physical, downhill linebacker with length, straight-line speed and the willingness to take on blockers, although his lateral stiffness and coverage limitations were significant concerns.Dugger has become a valuable part of San Francisco's defense, playing more than half the defensive snaps and recording 30 tackles through seven games. A former safety still learning the nuances of off-ball LB, he's making excellent use of his range, closing speed and versatility, with the coaching staff trusting him in coverage and as a blitzer. Also goes to show that sometimes one person's evaluation can miss the mark (and sometimes by a good bit).Kendal Daniels, LB, Falcons (Round 4): B+My pre-draft grade: 4th round | Final big board rank: No. 134Why I liked him: A versatile hybrid defender with outstanding range, physicality and some of the best open-field tackling ability in the class, capable of making plays from the slot, box or edge.One of my 2026 draft sleepers, Daniels has been one of the most impressive Day 3 picks of the class, starting all eight games with 53 tackles, four tackles for loss, a sack and an interception. His range, versatility and ability to finish tackles in space were among the reasons I thought he might sneak into Day 2, and he's already becoming an important part of Jeff Ulbrich's defense.

        Every week now, it seems like we are having to reevaluate the tight position in terms of who is a must-start, who is a borderline start, and who is an avoid. This week is no different. One way to look at it is by who has done what year-to-date, and in the most recent month. That's where we will start the Week 9 preview.As a rule, I use 12 PPR Fantasy points per game as a barometer for a must-start tight end. So far this year, six tight ends have hit that mark: Brock Bowers, Trey McBride, Isaiah Likely, George Kittle, Tyler Warren, and Sam LaPorta. If you wanted to call all of them must-starts, I wouldn't argue with you. Harold Fannin and Travis Kelce just miss the mark, but they are in the conversation.Looking at the last month, you'll find Colston Loveland (14.0), Kyle Pitts (13.5), and Tucker Kraft (13.1) join the mix while LaPorta falls out. We are mostly buying the recent surge from Loveland and Kraft, and we're content to give LaPorta one more week to break out of his slump, because he's facing the Dolphins. The one that is really hard to figure is Pitts.Since Michael Penix took over at QB, Pitts is averaging 10.5 PPR FPPG. But that is mostly about touchdowns. In the same stretch, he ranks 13th in receptions and 18th in yards at tight end despite not having a bye or missing a game. He has the same number of yards as AJ Barner and the same number of catches as Dallas Goedert, who has only played four games in the last six weeks.
All of that is to say, as big of a Pitts proponent as I was coming into the year, I don't view him as one of the must-start options and as of Tuesday afternoon, he is not one of my top 12 tight ends for Week 9. I also don't really want to drop him, so if you can't roster two tight ends, you should probably just start him and hope for a touchdown.Here's everything else you need to know about tight end in Week 9:

The two exceptions were supposed to be Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price, but injuries and time-shares have kept them from fully showing their talents in the NFL. In Week 8, a couple of different rookie running backs took over their backfields and this seems like a good time to talk about what we can expect from them moving forward.Jonah Coleman and Mike Washington both dominated the touches in Week 8, with different results. Coleman turned 15 touches into 16.4 PPR points while Washington's 25 touches produced just 8.3 points. There were two big differences: Efficiency and targets. Washington continued the trend of inefficiency from the lead back in Las Vegas, and averaged 3.3 yards per carry. He also had zero targets. Coleman caught four passes in Week 8, which is one more catch than Washington has all season.I don't think it is far-fetched to say that Washington could be a better rusher than Coleman, but the environment in Denver is so much better than the environment in Las Vegas. And the fact that Ashton Jeanty is still handling passing downs nukes Washington's PPR upside, while Coleman's backfield mate J.K. Dobbins is really only a threat on early downs. For that reason, Coleman is inside my top 20 running backs this week and may be for the rest of the season. body:
Joe Burrow, Patrick Mahomes and 10 other prominent players would have to approve any trade before the Nov. 10 deadline, but one quarterback may have reason to listen
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 3, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:46 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Everyone is trying to figure out which NFL players will be traded before the Nov. 10 deadline. While trades will inevitably happen, there are several players who certainly won't be dealt over the next week. Specifically, there are 12 players who most likely won't be traded as their contract currently includes a no-trade clause. For any of those players to be traded, they would first have to agree to a trade. Here's a rundown of the dozen players that most likely won't be traded, unless they waive their no-trade clause. DE Will Anderson, Texans
Even if the Texans were considering dealing Anderson (they aren't), his no-trade clause would make that difficult. Anderson is in the first season of his massive, three-year contract, and the Texans, despite a disappointing start, don't appear to be heading into rebuild mode. Anderson has gone consecutive games without a sack, but he still leads the NFL with 7.5 quarterback takedowns through eight weeks. Anderson's 16.5 sacks since Week 6 of the 2025 season is the third-most in the NFL over that span (behind only Myles Garrett and Chase Young). 
QB Joe Burrow, Bengals 
There's a better chance of astronauts landing on Jupiter next week than the Bengals trading Burrow, who is signed through the 2029 season. The soon-to-be 30-year-old Burrow is having an MVP-caliber season and is the biggest reason for the Bengals' 5-2 start. The former Heisman Trophy winner currently leads the NFL in completion percentage and touchdown passes. Burrow threw five touchdowns in Sunday's come-from-behind win over the Titans. DL Myles Garrett
Burrow was the quarterback Garrett sacked in Week 18 of the 2025 season to secure the NFL's all-time single-season sack record. That remains still Garrett's most recent sack, as he has been on the shelf since suffering an injury in Week 1. 
Garrett appears to be nearing his return; Rams coach Sean McVay said on Monday that the team will open his 21-day return window this week. QB Jared Goff, Lions 
Goff, who was famously traded from Los Angeles to Detroit back in 2021, has enjoyed a career resurgence with the Lions. It's been the perfect marriage of player and team. In Detroit, Goff helped restore the roar for a franchise that hadn't done much winning prior to his arrival. Goff has also become one of the league's most prolific passers since being traded. Barring injury, he will pass Hall of Famer Dan Fouts on the NFL's career passing list by season's end. He's three touchdown passes away from passing Hall of Famer Joe Montana on the all-time list. 
QB Justin Herbert, Chargers 
Of all the players on this list, Herbert is the player with the best chance of a trade. That would require Herbert to agree to waive his no-trade clause. Would he? It's hard to know, but it's possible that Herbert would at least consider it if a contending team with a solid offensive line and skill players came calling. One team that comes to mind are the Vikings, who are 6-1 despite getting average play from the quarterback position. Kyler Murray is dealing with a hamstring injury that could hinder his play moving forward. QB Jalen Hurts, Eagles 
Unfortunately for Hurts, he is dealing with something way more serious than football. Hurts is expected to miss the remainder of the season after blood clots were found in his lungs last month. Fortunately, the Eagles said that his prognosis is "very good" and that he is expected to make a full recovery.
QB Lamar Jackson, Ravens 
Jackson may also miss the remainder of the season after suffering a right thumb injury during Sunday's loss to the Bills. Even if Jackson was healthy, there was virtually no chance that he was going anywhere this season. His injury does, however, raise questions about his long-term future in Baltimore. Jackson's current contract runs through next season. He will be 31 years old when his current deal is set to expire. QB Trevor Lawrence, Jaguars 
Lawrence is in the midst of his finest NFL season. He's enjoying his highest completion percentage since 2022 and has thrown at least three touchdown passes four times. Lawrence leads the NFL in several categories that includes passer rating (112.6) and average yards gained per pass attempt. 
Lawrence has also dramatically cut down on his mistakes with just four interceptions so far. This has all contributed to Jacksonville's 5-2 start. QB Patrick Mahomes, Chiefs 
While the Chiefs have lost two straight after a 5-0 start, Mahomes has continued to play well. He threw for 321 yards and three touchdowns (while completing 73.2% of his passes) during Sunday's close loss to the Broncos. Mahomes is playing closer to his former MVP self this season. He's enjoying his highest passer rating since 2022, when he won his second league/Super Bowl MVP. 
QB Dak Prescott, Cowboys
While Prescott continues to put up numbers, the Cowboys continue to pile up losses. Dallas is 3-5 despite having an offense that is seventh in the league in points scored. Prescott has been at the forefront of that production with 14 touchdown passes and a league-high 108 passing first downs. Prescott's success this season made the Cowboys' decision to call 39 runs during Sunday's loss to the Cardinals all the more perplexing. QB Brock Purdy, 49ers 
Purdy continues to be one of the league's most underappreciated stars. He's playing at an MVP level this season, which has been one of the main reasons for the 49ers' 6-1 start. Purdy paces the NFL in several categories that includes QBR and passing success rate. 
Believe it or not, Purdy actually has the highest career passer rating (104.8) in NFL history. He won't, however, get his due respect until he leads the 49ers to a Super Bowl title. QB Deshaun Watson, Browns 
Watson is trying to make the most of the final year of his contract in Cleveland. The former Pro Bowler has played well enough to help the Browns get off to a 5-3 start. Watson has thrown over 300 yards in each of the Browns' last two games. Watson threw for a season-high 324 yards this past Sunday in Pittsburgh, but he also sacked eight times in an eventual 27-6 loss. Watson's 33 sacks leads the NFL.

There was some irritation at the fact that he did it all himself, hurting Colston Loveland and Luther Burden, but the general consensus was that Williams had arrived as an elite QB in Fantasy Football. Then he pulled his hamstring in Week 2 and didn't play again until Week 6. In the three games since, Williams has played the best football of his career; the Bears are 3-0 with wins over both of last year's Super Bowl participants. Everything is awesome again, right? Well, it has been for Bears fans, not so much for Williams' Fantasy managers. In his last three games, Williams has averaged 20.2 Fantasy points per game, which would be tied with Matthew Stafford for QB15 on the season. The Fantasy "problem" is a lack of rushing and a lack of touchdowns. He has 22 yards rushing and four total touchdowns in those three games. For the season, the Bears rank 26th in the NFL with eight passing TDs and second in the league with 17 rushing touchdowns. That makes some sense, considering the Bears have a 62.3% red-zone rush rate, the third-highest mark in the league.This all leads to the question of what to do with Williams in Week 9. The Bears face a Tampa Bay defense that suddenly looks imposing. They have a top-five defense in points and yards allowed, and a top-10 defense against both the run and the pass. This is no easy matchup. Which is another reason why, in my early Week 9 projections, Williams projects as QB16. Certainly not a must-start QB, but also projected to outscore every QB available on the waiver wire. If you are carrying two good QBs, there is a good chance I would sit Williams this week.
